item.title: Understanding Commitment Uncertainty in Relationships
item.description:
Relationships

Understanding Commitment Uncertainty in Relationships

Helping couples decide whether to stay together or separate.

Posted October 14, 2026

Key points
  • Commitment can involve both dedication and constraints that keep partners together.
  • Commitment uncertainty can exist at the outset, or develop after an event or as the relationship deteriorates.
  • Both attachment anxiety and attachment avoidance are associated with relationship uncertainty.
  • Commitment uncertainty can concern one's own commitment or their perception of their partner’s commitment.

Commitment uncertainty is one of the major challenges couples may present with in couples therapy. Commitment is typically a fundamental part of an exclusive romantic relationship. It influences how partners invest in the relationship, identify with one another, and engage with their shared life. Yet, partners may become unsure whether they want to remain committed, whether the relationship will continue, or whether they want to keep investing in it. This is referred to as commitment uncertainty. Understanding this uncertainty is important because a lack of commitment is strongly associated with separation and divorce.

Commitment uncertainty emerges after partners have formed a mutually agreed-upon relationship, such as an exclusive monogamous relationship, and it differs from the uncertainty that can occur during early dating, when the relationship status has not yet been defined.

What Is Commitment?

Several theoretical models describe two broad aspects of commitment. The first concerns wanting to be in the relationship, while the second concerns forces that encourage a person to remain in the relationship.

Research distinguishes these as dedication commitment and constraint commitment. Dedication includes a strong sense of couple identity, a desire for the relationship to continue long term, giving the relationship priority, and a willingness to sacrifice for it. As partners experience their relationship as meaningful and meeting their needs, they tend to pay less attention to alternatives. Constraint commitment refers to difficulties that bind partners together. These can include investments in the relationship, concerns about the well-being of a partner or children, financial circumstances, and social pressure. Constraints can encourage partners to remain together and may also encourage them to work on their relationship. However, constraint commitment alone is unlikely to be sufficient for a functional and healthy relationship in the long term.

How Commitment Uncertainty Develops

Supported by research findings, my experience as a licensed psychologist counselling individuals and couples from all over the world revealed several ways in which commitment uncertainty can emerge in an intimate relationship.

A Significant Relationship Event

Uncertainty may begin with an event that becomes a

Source: Diana Tutschek

turning point in the relationship. Such an event can lead partners to reevaluate their relationship and its future.

A Gradual Deterioration

Commitment uncertainty may also develop slowly as connection and engagement between partners deteriorate. At the same time, partners may avoid confronting their uncertainty. Existing constraints, such as living together or having children, can help sustain the relationship and make it possible for partners to resist the growing uncertainty.

Recognition of Compatibility Issues

In other cases, commitment uncertainty may become apparent without a specific event. Partners may recognise fundamental compatibility problems and realise that critical issues in the relationship were not adequately considered earlier.

Uncertainty From the Beginning

For some couples, uncertainty may have been present from the beginning of the relationship. A relationship may begin with low levels of adjustment and remain consistently low in adjustment.

Commitment Uncertainty Due to Attachment Insecurity

Furthermore, there is a critical factor associated with commitment uncertainty: attachment insecurity, comprised of two dimensions, attachment anxiety and attachment avoidance. Relationship uncertainty is known to mediate the association between both attachment dimensions and commitment.

However, the two attachment dimensions are associated with uncertainty in different ways.

Attachment anxiety involves a strong desire for intimacy and protection alongside concerns about a partner's availability and commitment, fear of abandonment, and concerns about one's own value to the partner. Increasing attachment anxiety is also associated with jealousy and greater emotional ups and downs.

Attachment avoidance, on the other hand, involves discomfort with closeness and dependence, less reliance on relationship partners for care, and a preference for distance. Lower trust in partners and perceptions of others as negative or unreliable are seen as factors associated with increased doubts about the relationship.

The indirect association with commitments was stronger for attachment anxiety than for attachment avoidance.

Why Can Commitment Uncertainty Persist?

Both external and internal factors can contribute to the persistence of commitment uncertainty.

External constraints can make it difficult to act on uncertainty. Concern about children, for example, may encourage partners to remain together and attempt to work through their difficulties. Financial constraints may have a similar effect. These pressures can help couples remain together while facing uncertainty, but they can also result in partners staying together without addressing the underlying uncertainty, potentially contributing to increasing negativity in the long term.

Internal processes can also interfere with fully addressing uncertainty. Denial, dissociation, and avoidance may reduce contact with the emotional turmoil associated with uncertainty. Such processes may also be expressed behaviourally, including through an affair.

Assessing Commitment Uncertainty in Couples Therapy

First of all, commitment uncertainty can concern either a person’s own commitment to the relationship or their perception of their partner’s commitment.

Secondly, it is useful to consider dedication and constraint commitment, as these different aspects can help clarify the nature of the couple's commitment and how it developed.

For example, a feeling of having been trapped by circumstances may indicate that commitment was not fully established initially and may contribute to continuing uncertainty.

During a course of my integrative couples therapy, online or in person, I tend to discuss commitment uncertainty during joint sessions and explore it further in individual sessions, while establishing clear boundaries and explicit confidentiality arrangements from the outset.

Chicken or Egg Dilemma: Commitment or Relationship Change?

A particularly difficult situation arises when couples describe their position as: “I would be more committed if things improved.” The “things” may include communication, intimacy, or other difficulties within the relationship.

This creates a “chicken-and-egg” dilemma. A partner may say that commitment will follow improvement, while the lack of commitment itself reduces motivation to change relationship behaviour.

There may be two possible ways of addressing this dilemma. The couple may directly address whether the relationship should continue, or they may temporarily put the question of commitment aside and work on other relationship difficulties.

Some couples may agree to set aside questions about continuing the relationship for a set period. This can provide stability while they work on the relationship and prevent the possibility of separation from becoming a bargaining tool during everyday disagreements.

If the purpose of couples therapy is instead to clarify the future of the relationship, commitment itself needs to remain central to the work. The process involves examining the factors influencing the decision, considering the consequences of staying or leaving, and distinguishing relationship distress from a desire to end the relationship.

What Is the Goal of Couples Therapy That Addresses Commitment Uncertainty?

Traditional measures of successful couples therapy often focus on improved relationship functioning or avoiding separation or divorce. However, for couples experiencing commitment uncertainty, remaining together is not necessarily the only possible outcome of therapy. The outcome may include separating well or achieving satisfactory individual well-being.

I find it important to focus couples therapy on reducing avoidance and increasing positive engagement with the question of commitment.

In addition, couples therapy should not rush towards a decision. A demand for certainty may itself represent avoidance; thus, space for thoughtful decision-making needs to be allowed.

To sum up, for couples experiencing commitment uncertainty, therapy may involve exploring how that uncertainty developed, what maintains it, and what they want the outcome of therapy to be.

item.title: When Your Cofounder Partnership No Longer Fits
item.description:
Coaching

When Your Cofounder Partnership No Longer Fits

Unspoken deals between founders can break quietly when one partner grows.

Posted October 14, 2026

Key points
  • Cofounders often form an unspoken deal about roles and power in their first months together.
  • When one partner grows, that deal can stop fitting, and the conflict moves to safer topics.
  • The same strain can feel like constriction to one partner and betrayal to the other.
  • One plain-language conversation can update the deal and change how decisions get made.
Source: Dall-E/OpenAI

For the cofounder who has outgrown the partnership, it feels tight. You notice yourself getting smaller in meetings. You wonder whether the partnership is worth it. Eventually you stop giving feedback, because what's the point, and the resentment piles up. People in this seat often leave.

A friend of mine lived a version of this. He was carrying most of his company's day-to-day operations when he walked away.

On the surface, the conflict with his two partners concerned go-to-market strategy, and they had debated it repeatedly without resolution. Underneath those debates was a shift in an agreement the three of them had never stated aloud.

The Deal Nobody Says Out Loud

When he joined the company, his partners were roughly 20 years his senior, considerably more experienced, and already financially successful. He was early in his career and still working toward his first million.

The terms of their arrangement were never written down, yet all three understood them. He would defer to their judgment, and their opinions would carry more weight. They would serve as his mentors, and he would turn their ideas into a functioning product.

His partners found meaning in the mentor role—giving back to a younger founder was gratifying for them. He received an education he could not have purchased, and in exchange he declined other opportunities and accepted reduced income while the company was not yet profitable. For the first few years, the arrangement held.

In Marital Tensions (1967), the psychiatrist Henry Dicks, drawing on his work with couples at London's Tavistock Clinic, described what he called unconscious working agreements: unspoken contracts shaped by how two partners' needs and defenses fit together. Neither partner designs such an agreement intentionally, yet both maintain it. Dicks termed this shared maintenance collusion, a word that refers to joint participation, largely outside of awareness.

Founders often describe the beginning of a partnership as chemistry. Some of that synergy reflects genuine liking for one another and complementary skill sets. Some of it reflects two sets of unconscious needs fitting together, and those needs change over time.

When One Partner Outgrows It

Two or three years in, my friend had internalized how his partners thought and began developing views of his own. He was also carrying a disproportionate share of the operational load, which tends to sharpen one's opinions quickly. He came to see their go-to-market thinking as outdated, and he said so.

The original agreement had no room for that. It had been built for a junior partner, and he no longer occupied that role.

This is the dynamic founders tend to underestimate. They revisit equity and titles as the company matures. But the unspoken agreement rarely receives the same attention, largely because no one remembers entering into it.

For the partners on the other side, the change can register as betrayal, as though someone were breaking terms that were never stated. What they are losing may be something they would never admit to needing, such as being looked up to. Between one partner's constriction and the other's sense of betrayal, an honest conversation becomes considerably harder to begin.

So why does a shift in power show up as a fight about a business-related issue? Because that topic is safe to talk about. Most partnerships run on operational language: targets, roadmaps, tasks. Talking about status and need requires a different vocabulary, and using it requires vulnerability.

For my friend, the honest version would have sounded something like this: I've learned a lot from you, I now disagree with you on some big things, and I need that to be okay. Saying that aloud carries genuine interpersonal risk, but creates the opportunity for the group to evolve.

Instead, he challenged their strategy. Because he never named the shift in power, his objections did not land, and eventually he left.

Updating the Deal

These deals are hard to see from the inside. One useful clue is a reaction that's out of proportion to the issue. You replay the meeting at night. You vent to your spouse, your friends, your coach. That intensity often means something under the surface is asking to be updated.

Therapists who practice acceptance and commitment therapy sometimes describe two climbers on separate mountains. From across the valley, I can spot the boulder on your trail more easily than you can, and you can spot mine. Cofounders are climbing the same mountain, which is part of why an outside view from a specialist helps.

Before you talk to your cofounder, it helps to get honest with yourself. Think back to when you started. What were you counting on them for? Energy, encouragement, being the one who knew more? And what did you quietly offer in return? Some of those terms probably still fit. Some were written for people you no longer are.

Then have one conversation, in plain language. You don't need clinical terms, and you don't need to be a therapist. Open by saying you'd like to talk about the recent disagreements and about how the partnership itself has changed, and that you want to hear their view too. Then speak for yourself: Say what has changed in you, and that you know it has created friction. Then ask what they've noticed.

From there, make one concrete change to how you decide things, such as who has the final call in which areas. Try it, then adjust. Write it down, and look at it again in a year. The original deal may never become fully conscious, and that's fine. What matters is that the partnership catches up to the people in it, so your next disagreement about the plan can actually be about the plan.

item.title: The Wild Unpredictability of Your Dreams
item.description:
Dreaming

The Wild Unpredictability of Your Dreams

The experience of pure freedom in dreaming is a reminder of who you really are.

Posted October 14, 2026

Key points
  • Dreams are like subatomic particles in being fundamentally unpredictable.
  • Each dream offers an experience of limitless possibility and spontaneous creativity.
  • Dreams resist social pressures that threaten the innate freedom of human life.
Source: Kelly Bulkeley

A curious paradox confronts dream researchers today. New technologies of data analysis allow us to identify large-scale patterns in dream content with more precision than ever before. At the same time, it remains true that each dream is a unique and free creation of the imagination in sleep, spontaneously emergent and incapable of being predicted. In short, we find consistency in general dreaming and wildness in individual dreams.

Although disconcerting to researchers, this paradox is a psychological blessing in disguise, especially for anyone interested in learning about the nature of the human mind and its potential for new growth in even the most perilous of conditions.

Dreams and Subatomic Particles

Those of us who study dreams are now able to make highly accurate predictions about the general patterns in people’s dreams. With a large enough data set, we can identify recurrent patterns in dream content and predict the frequency of their future occurrence, along with their relevance to the dreamer’s waking life. The discovery of these recurrent patterns is a major advance in dream science, refuting the sceptic’s tiresome claim that dreams are nothing more than random nonsense.

However, it also remains true that we cannot predict with the same precision the contents of any particular dream. If someone gave us 100 dream reports, we could generate an accurate profile of the major themes and patterns in their general dream life. But even if the person gave us 1,000 or more dreams, and we used the most powerful AI systems available, we still could not do more than guess what exactly they will dream about next.

This calls to mind the challenge facing physicists in dealing with quantum indeterminacy, in which they are unable to measure the exact location of any one subatomic particle. Physicists can accurately measure the probabilities of where the particle might be, and this allows them to build general models of objective validity. But those models do not and, according to the strongest version of quantum physics, cannot determine the exact location of any particular subatomic particle. There is a fundamental and irreducible unpredictability woven into the fabric of physical reality.

Something similar seems to be true in dream science, where we can predict with remarkable accuracy the broad themes of people’s dreams over time, but not what they will dream about on any given night. Even people who practice dream incubation rituals are only making a sincere request of their dreams, not a command of obedience. With its uncanny freedom and stubborn autonomy, the dreaming imagination will either respond to the incubation request or it won’t, and there is nothing else to be done about it.

The Gifts of Dreaming

This seemingly contradictory quality of dreaming—predictable in its long-term patterns, unpredictable in its individual instances—offers a double gift to anyone who is willing to listen to what their dreams have to say.

First, the long-term patterns of your dreams can reveal in surprising detail the emotional network of your most important concerns in waking life. Learning more about these oneiric patterns can provide intriguing insights into your relationships, health, work and finances, cultural interests, and even religious and political beliefs. Such deeply rooted insights can be invaluable for personal growth or any kind of therapeutic practice.

Second, each individual dream offers you an amazing gift: an experience of wildness, freedom, and spontaneous creativity. In addition to whatever personal meanings you can interpret in its contents, each dream reveals to you a realm of pure imaginal play, a realm that is your natural home every time you fall asleep. Within that realm you experience what it is to live an unbounded, unpredictable, irreducibly wild existence. It makes this gift even more amazing to know that it is shared by everyone, everywhere. Each human has the innate capacity in and through their dreams to experience the free spirit of wide-open possibility.

Opposing Forces

In our strange and troubled world of today, this latter gift holds special importance, because several recent trends are pushing in exactly the opposite direction. For instance, neuroscience tell us our mental activities and sense of self are entirely determined by brain chemistry. Social media algorithms have gained a frightening power to shape our collective fears and desires. The rise of AI seems to diminish to near insignificance the scope and dignity of human creativity. And looming over all, climate change threatens the natural ecosystem of our entire planet.

This dire external context highlights even more clearly the value of dreaming as a universally accessible source of inner wildness. Dreams liberate our minds from conventional viewpoints, give us new ways of seeing reality, and imagine alternative visions of the future, all of which directly strengthens our capacity to resist conforming to oppressive patterns of thought and behavior. Against the dehumanizing forces of current society, the playful autonomy and infinite expansion of possibility we experience in dreaming reminds us of who we truly are and what we always have the potential to become.

Wild Dreaming in Practice

In practice, this means trying to give special attention to the strangest, weirdest, most bizarre images and themes in your dreams. No need for interpretation or decoding, just focus on what it feels like to be the dreamer of such marvels. Do what you can to welcome these wild energies into your waking awareness and let them linger there as long as they want.

When people begin paying attention to their dreams, it often happens that their dreams start paying more attention to them, responding to their interest with a vibrant stream of spontaneous imagery and feeling. You can help this process by keeping a dream journal, sharing dreams with other trusted people, and doing whatever you can to carry the endlessly dynamic energies of your dreams into the waking world.

item.title: Why Loneliness Doesn’t Always Need to Be Cured
item.description:
Loneliness

Why Loneliness Doesn’t Always Need to Be Cured

Loneliness can be painful and meaningful, and may require different responses.

Posted October 14, 2026

Key points
  • Treating all loneliness as pathology can add shame and obscure what the experience means.
  • Loneliness takes different forms, shaped by bereavement, exclusion, illness, and life transitions.
  • Persistent loneliness can damage health and functioning, while still carrying personal meaning.
  • Effective responses begin by understanding a particular loneliness and what has produced it.

“People tell me I come across as anything but lonely,” Eva told me when I interviewed her for The Loneliness Project.

Others saw her as a “strong, energetic and independent woman,” she assured me. They did not see the shame beneath the veneer — the loneliness that had quietly accompanied her since her husband’s death.

They had been married for twenty-five years. Without him, she told me, she no longer knew where she fit or who she was.

“Oh, I definitely carry a sense of inadequacy and shame about feeling so lonely,” she explained. “I’ll act the part, but often with an inner terror that if I let my guard slip, the loneliness will show.”

It struck me that she was deeply ashamed of her loneliness. Somehow, she understood it as a personal failure, something that separated her from others.

I’m increasingly convinced that experiences like Eva’s are partly the cost of a dominant narrative around loneliness. Psychologist Dolores Albarracín and colleagues have argued that there has been a tendency to pathologize, diagnose, and seek to “cure” difficult psychological experiences that may be fundamental parts of being alive.

Loneliness is not treated any differently. Increasingly, it is described as a public health crisis, a pathology to be treated, or a defect to be eradicated.

My concerns centre around two arguments: (1) framing loneliness as primarily pathological risks breeding shame and secrecy around it; and (2) what if loneliness often arises as a deeply human response to life?

The Public Health Narrative

It helps to examine how loneliness has come to be spoken about at the highest levels of public authority and in culture.

One of the most influential interventions came from Vivek Murthy, then United States Surgeon General. In 2023, Murthy issued an advisory on what he called an epidemic of loneliness. The report warned that the mortality impact of insufficient social connection is comparable to smoking up to fifteen cigarettes a day. By such logic, loneliness is primarily viewed as a health risk, while its emotional and existential meaning can shrink from view.

Of course, we have much for which to thank this narrative. For much of history, loneliness has remained confined to private inner life. People haven’t had the language or permission to speak about it. Its emergence as a public-health concern has helped to bring such suffering to light. Without this, governments and institutions would find it easier to look past loneliness.

The public-health narrative has also encouraged researchers to examine the relationship between loneliness and sleep, stress, cardiovascular health, depression, cognitive decline, and mortality. Whatever complexities surround these associations, they should not be dismissed. For some people, loneliness is an entrenched and painful condition that constricts their world and dampens well-being.

Symptom or Signal?

But for all the good it does, the public-health narrative also shifts our focus from understanding why loneliness has appeared, and searching for its meaning, to assuming meaning a priori. The emphasis shifts from understanding why loneliness has appeared in someone’s life — and what it may mean — to focusing predominantly on its elimination.

Loneliness becomes a symptom, rather than a signal.

When we approach something as a symptom, we tend to assume it is evidence that something has gone wrong. Symptoms often point us towards deficits, malfunction, disorder, and pathology.

Signals occupy a different category. A signal is not necessarily evidence of dysfunction. It is informational and tells us that something important is taking place that we may want to pay attention to.

In my research, I have often found that when we listen to a person’s loneliness, it can point toward meaningful absence, threatened connection, unlived possibility, neglected relationships, a hidden part of the Self seeking expression, or significant life transition. In these examples, the experience remains painful, but the meaning of the pain changes.

Pain Is Not the Same as Pathology

Loneliness is not a uniform state. It varies in intensity, duration, origin, meaning, and consequence. The important distinction is not between loneliness that hurts and loneliness that doesn't. In my experience, almost all loneliness hurts.

For example, grief can be excruciating without constituting illness. A period of profound loneliness after bereavement may be painful precisely because the relationship that has been lost was deeply significant.

At times, loneliness can impair sleep, motivation, self-care, relationships, and a person’s capacity to participate in life. And when it becomes entangled with sustained despair, serious functional decline, or thoughts of self-harm or death, it should never be treated simply as an interesting existential message. Understanding is important, but so is care, protection, companionship, and appropriate professional support.

What Does Loneliness Need?

The loneliness arising from bereavement asks something very different of us from the loneliness produced by exclusion. The loneliness of feeling unseen by those we are closest to may not require the same response as loneliness rooted in illness or the gradual disappearance of someone’s social world.

This requires what I like to call loneliness literacy; the capacity to recognise loneliness in its different forms, understand it in the context of a person’s life, and discern what kind of response it requires. The task is to understand a particular loneliness before deciding what should be done about it.

Eva did not need to be persuaded that her loneliness was beneficial. She was grieving a man she had loved for twenty-five years and was trying to discover who she was without him. She had lost the map by which she had navigated life. Her loneliness was testimony to love, loss, and a profound need for connection. It also pointed towards a new identity and a life that was being painfully reconfigured.

What compounded her suffering, however, was the story that feeling lonely meant something was wrong with her — that she was somehow "less than" because of it.

Not every loneliness needs to be cured. But all loneliness deserves to be understood.

I write more about loneliness, connection, and the quieter dimensions of inner life at The Inner Room.
